issues.description: There is a discrepancy in the reported effect size for the original study's 'Advantageous' outcome. Table 1 reports a standardized beta of -.300, while Table 3 reports an original r of -0.33. This inconsistency undermines the accuracy of the meta-analytic comparisons.
issues.quote: Original | Forest & Wood | 80 | ... | -.300 | .011 [Table 1] vs Original r | Advantageous | -0.33 [Table 3]

issues.description: Table 1 lists the original study's beta for 'Express' as 'n/a', yet Table 3 provides an 'Original r' of 0.15 for this same construct. The manuscript does not explain how this value was derived or where it was sourced from if it was not in the original publication.
issues.quote: The original study did not report a beta coefficient for this variable. [Table 1 Note] vs Express | Original r | 0.15 [Table 3]

issues.description: The authors state that 'Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient.' This is only true in simple linear regression with a single predictor. If any of the models included covariates or multiple predictors, using beta as a direct proxy for r is statistically incorrect.
issues.quote: Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient.

issues.description: One of the replication studies (Gordon) summed the items for the composite score, while others averaged them. In a meta-analysis of correlations, using different scaling methods (sums vs. means) can affect the variance and the resulting correlation coefficients if not properly standardized.
issues.quote: The means for scores in most studies implied that the items were mean averaged, but the Gordon study’s mean implied items were summed.

issues.description: The authors admit they do not know the procedures for handling missing data for all studies because analysis scripts were not always provided. This represents a significant 'researcher degree of freedom' that could introduce unsystematic error into the meta-analysis.
issues.quote: Contributors did not always post analysis scripts, so procedures to account for missing data are not known for all studies.

issues.description: The use of the Fail-Safe Number (FSN) is widely discouraged in modern meta-analytic practice as it is highly sensitive to the effect sizes of the included studies and does not actually measure publication bias effectively.
issues.quote: Finally, we conducted a fail-safe number (FSN) analysis (Rosenberg, 2005) using the fsn function.

issues.description: The Rosenberg Self-Esteem (RSE) scale was administered using a 4-point scale in some studies and a 5-point scale in others (IIT-Sp16, IIT-Sp17). Mixing different response scales for the primary predictor without testing for measurement invariance or using a standardized mean difference approach is problematic.
issues.quote: most replications used the original four-point scale, while two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point scale.

issues.description: The studies mixed online and in-lab administration. Furthermore, one study (SAU) ran participants in groups, while others ran them individually. Social presence is a known confound in studies regarding social media perceptions and self-disclosure.
issues.quote: researchers employed both methods (three replications had participants complete in lab only, two used online only, and two used both methods)... SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six.

issues.description: In Table 3, for the 'Advantageous' outcome in the BYU-Sp16 study, the difference between the replication r (-0.02) and original r (-0.33) is listed as -0.31. Mathematically, -0.02 - (-0.33) = +0.31. The sign is reversed, suggesting a calculation or entry error.

The authors report I^2 and Q statistics for a meta-analysis with only 7 studies. Heterogeneity estimates are known to be highly biased and underpowered when k < 10, making these values unreliable for interpretation.
issues.quote: The between-study variance in the replication studies did not appear to be heterogenous, Q(df = 6) = 4.75, p = .576; T2 = 0... I2 = 0%

issues.description: Regarding the 'Express' outcome, the authors state there was a 'lack of an effect,' yet they also note that the 95% Prediction Interval (PI) did not include zero [.01, .14]. If the PI excludes zero, it suggests a consistent, albeit small, effect exists, contradicting the 'null' conclusion.
issues.quote: The PI came close to, but did not include, zero so it may be that there is an effect... led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect.

issues.description: The authors acknowledge that Facebook usage patterns changed significantly between 2012 and 2017. This is not just a discussion point but a fundamental threat to the construct validity of a 'direct replication,' as the platform itself (the stimulus) evolved.
issues.quote: Participants in our replication studies may have been implicitly comparing Facebook usage to Snapchat and Instagram... whereas these platforms would not have been a consideration for participants in Forest and Wood’s (2012) study.

issues.description: The study relies entirely on undergraduate students from the US. While this matches the original study, the manuscript overclaims the generalizability of the findings to 'Facebook users' or 'people' in general without sufficient caveats about the WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) nature of the sample.
issues.quote: The results provided further evidence regarding the original study’s generalizability and robustness.

issues.description: Demographic data, particularly race, was not collected for the majority of the replication studies. This prevents any analysis of whether the effects are moderated by cultural or ethnic backgrounds, which the authors later speculate about in the discussion.
issues.quote: in all other studies no other demographic information was collected because the original Forest and Wood (2012) research did not indicate any other demographic information was collected

issues.description: The authors use correlational, cross-sectional data to support Social Compensation Theory, which is inherently a process-oriented/causal theory. The data cannot confirm if Facebook *mitigates* anxiety, only that self-esteem correlates with perceptions.
issues.quote: This theory suggests that for those with lower self-esteem, the anxiety provoked by FTF interactions can be somewhat mitigated in online interactions. However, the CREP studies did not include a measure of FTF vs. online anxiety

issues.description: The authors suggest that p-values between .04 and .05 are more likely under a true null hypothesis. This is a controversial interpretation of p-value distributions (p-hacking vs. true effect) and is used to dismiss the original study's finding on 'Connection' without sufficient evidence.
issues.quote: p-values between .04 and .05 have been demonstrated to be relatively more likely in the case of a true null hypothesis than a false one

issues.description: Table 3 contains redundant column headers (e.g., 'Advantageous' repeated 6 times across the row) which makes the table difficult to parse and suggests a lack of final proofreading.
issues.quote: Advantageous | Advantageous | Advantageous | Advantageous | Advantageous | Advantageous [Table 3]

issues.description: The original study (N=80) was severely underpowered to detect the small-to-medium effects typically found in social psychology, especially for regression with multiple outcomes. The meta-analysis should more explicitly address how the original study's low power contributes to the 'disparity' in effect sizes.
issues.quote: This is primarily caused by the small sample size of the original study

issues.description: One study (IIT-Sp16) changed the wording of 40% of the RSE items. Even minor wording changes can alter the psychometric properties of a validated scale, potentially affecting the correlation with other variables.
issues.quote: one study (IIT-Sp16) had slight differences in item order and in wording on four out of ten items

issues.description: The authors conclude that it is 'unlikely' future studies will find an effect for 'Connection' because the PI includes zero. However, the PI is [-0.07, 0.27], which is heavily skewed toward a positive effect, yet the original study found a negative effect (-0.22). The PI actually suggests the original effect is an outlier, not just that the effect is null.
issues.quote: We believe that it will be unlikely that future studies will find an effect similar to the original, supported by the 95% PI of [-.07, .27], which includes zero.
